title: The Oldest Rule
part: PART TWO: THE TOLL OF ONE STORY

pages.text:
*From the Bridgewater Almanac: The old bridge was built by the town's founders, with their own hands, and has never needed mending.*

Rain tapped against the moss on the old bridge, a steady, patient drumming that made the hollow under the arch feel like a cave inside a sleeping giant. Rue sat cross-legged on a flat stone, her rubber boots squelching slightly, while Hobb poured tea from a kettle that hummed a low, contented note.

"Tell me a story," Hobb said, his grey-green skin dusted with ferns, and he looked at Rue with round spectacles mended with twine. "A good one. I have paid in tea for the last four."

Rue sipped the tea, which tasted of honey and damp earth. "Right then," she said, because she was a little scared of how much she liked this. "The Mayor’s hat is missing its left feather. He says it flew away, but Biscuit saw it in the drain. And Cedric’s red waistcoat has a stain that looks suspiciously like jam."

Hobb laughed, a sound like a rock rolling down a hill. "And the older stories? The ones before the stones?"

Rue leaned forward. "The town says you ate the baker’s sheep."

"I did not eat the baker’s sheep," Hobb said, offended. "I was reading a novel. It had a very sad ending."
pages.image: A cozy hollow under a stone arch with rain dripping outside; a small freckled girl in a yellow raincoat sits cross-legged, while a large mossy troll with round twine-mended spectacles pours tea from a humming kettle.

pages.text:
"Before the bridge," Hobb said, his voice dropping to a soft murmur that matched the rain, "there was only a ford, where the mud got into everyone's boots and the huts smelled of woodsmoke." He traced a finger along the wet stone of the arch. "I was young then, much younger than I am now, and I lived under the water, lifting people up on the flood nights when the river got too angry."

"The founders wanted a real bridge, something made of stone that would last, but they could not build one without help." He paused, looking at the kettle. "So I offered a deal. I would build it, stone by stone, in the dark, while they slept. In return, they would pay a toll of one story to cross, and no one would ever look under it too closely."

Rue tilted her head. "Why wouldn’t they look?"

"Because," Hobb said, adjusting his spectacles, "I was shy, and I was tired, and I thought if they just walked over, they might forget I was there." He smiled a small, sad smile. "It was a fair deal, and nobody meant it to be forgotten."
pages.image: Hobb, the enormous gentle troll with a patched waistcoat and round mended spectacles, gestures toward a rough stone arch with a gentle nostalgic expression while rain streaks the background

pages.text:
"Three hundred years," Hobb said, tapping the stone beside him. "I have kept it standing. I re-seat the stones when the river shifts them. I unclog the drains when the silt builds up. I patch the cracks before they widen. The town thinks the bridge just doesn’t need mending. They say it is strong. They say it is old and wise."

He smiled, and the moss on his shoulders rippled. "That is the whole idea of a good bridge, isn't it? You walk across and you don't think about the person holding it up. You just get to the other side, dry and safe. It’s only a bridge. Somebody has to hold it up."

Rue looked at his hands, which were broad and rough as tree bark, and then at the smooth, dry stones of the arch. She thought of the long way round she had walked for years. She thought of the fear in the town’s eyes. "It’s a very heavy job," she said quietly.
pages.image: A wide view of the mossy troll's large hands resting on rough grey stone, with small green moss plants growing between his fingers; the background is a dim, quiet stone archway with soft light filtering in.

pages.text:
"Nobody pays," Rue said. She had been thinking about this. "If the toll is one story, why does nobody pay? Why do they just throw stones?"

Hobb’s ears, which were shaped like leaves, drooped slightly. He reached into his patched waistcoat and pulled out a long, twisted stick of wood. It was a tally stick, carved with notches. Most of the notches were worn smooth.

He pointed to a cluster of marks near the top. There were perhaps twenty of them, and then a jagged break in the wood, as if a piece had been snapped off.

"This was the last one," Hobb said. His voice was very quiet. "About sixty years ago. A girl came. She paid the toll. She told me a story I have not forgotten. And then she made me a promise."

Rue felt a cold prickle at the back of her neck. "What promise?"

Hobb did not answer. He looked at her, and his face did something that made Rue lower her gaze to her boots. He carefully put the stick back in his pocket.
pages.image: A close-up of a mossy troll's hand holding a long, rough wooden tally stick with carved notches and a jagged break; his expression is serious and slightly sad, with his round spectacles reflecting the dim light.

pages.text:
Rue climbed the steps out of the arch, the rain now a soft mist on her face. She held the question in her chest, and it felt heavy, like a marble she could not toss away. Who was the girl? What promise had she broken?

She knew, with a sudden, sharp certainty, who it was. Gran. Gran, with her flour on her sleeves and her locked drawer and her sharp tongue that was really just a shield. Gran, who had never once mentioned the toll, or the bridge, or the way the town spoke of the troll as if he were a bad dream.

Rue walked home, her boots slapping against the wet cobblestones. She did not run. She did not hide. She just walked, holding her head high, feeling the secret pressing hard against her ribs.

At the corner, Cedric Pettibone stepped out of a doorway. He wore his red waistcoat, and his hair was slicked back, and he was not sneering. He looked, for the first time, like a boy who was very small and very alone.

"I saw you on the old bridge," he said, very quietly.
pages.image: A small, freckled girl in a yellow raincoat and green yarn hair puffs stands on wet cobblestones, looking up at a skinny boy in a red waistcoat with slicked-back hair who steps out of a dark doorway.
